n: Chapter 23 is another blunt allegory, this time about two sisters. Like chapter 16, it uses the picture of marital unfaithfulness to show how deeply Israel’s idolatry and foreign alliances wounded her covenant with God.

f.w: The word of the LORD came again unto me

n: Two sisters, daughters of one mother, represent the two kingdoms that grew from one people, Israel.

f.w: two women, the daughters of one mother
f.g: Northern Israel and southern Judah, divided after Solomon.

n: Even in their youth in Egypt they were unfaithful—Israel adopted Egyptian idols before the Exodus.
Their names are Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem). Both belonged to God and bore him children—the people of each kingdom.

f.g: “Her tent”—perhaps implying Samaria had her own unauthorized shrines.
“My tent is in her”—God’s own sanctuary was in Jerusalem, making her betrayal worse.

n: Samaria, while still God’s, chased after her lovers, the Assyrians—seeking security through alliances rather than through God.
She was dazzled by Assyria’s impressive officers—uniformed, mounted, and powerful. Political glamour led her away.

f.g: Purple or blue garments, a sign of wealth and rank.

n: She gave herself to Assyria’s elite and defiled herself with their idols.

f.w: with all their idols she defiled herself

n: She never gave up the habits she began in Egypt.
So God handed her over to the very Assyrians she desired.

f.w: delivered her into the hand of her lovers

n: Assyria exposed and destroyed her, took her children captive, and killed her. Samaria became a byword among nations (722 BC).

f.g: Her fate became notorious.

n: Jerusalem saw what happened to her sister—yet became even more corrupt. Failing to learn from another’s example makes guilt greater.

f.w: she was more corrupt in her inordinate love than she

n: She too chased Assyria’s splendid officers—Judah’s King Ahaz famously asked Assyria for help.
God saw she was defiled and took the same path as her sister.

f.g: Both went the same way.

n: She went further: seeing pictures of Babylonian men painted in red on walls, she was attracted to Babylon as well.

f.g: A bright red pigment used in wall paintings.

n: These images showed Babylonian officers in fine belts and flowing headdresses—the look of an impressive empire.

f.g: Flowing, colorful turbans.

n: As soon as she saw them she was infatuated and sent messengers to Babylon. Judah’s kings did court Babylon’s favor.

f.w: sent messengers unto them into Chaldea

n: The Babylonians came, defiled her, and then she grew disgusted with them—Judah later rebelled against Babylon.

f.w: her mind was alienated from them
f.g: She turned away from them in disgust.

n: Her shamelessness was public, and God turned away from her as he had from her sister.

f.w: my mind was alienated from her

n: Yet she went back to Egypt, remembering her youth—Zedekiah turned to Egypt for help against Babylon.

f.w: in calling to remembrance the days of her youth

n: She lusted after Egypt with crude, animal-like desire. Ezekiel’s coarse imagery is meant to shock readers into seeing how degrading their trust in Egypt was.

f.g: Lovers; here Egypt’s rulers.

n: She longed again for the corruption of her youth in Egypt.

f.g: Israel’s idolatry dating back to Egypt.

n: Now God will raise up those very lovers—the Babylonians she had grown disgusted with—against her from every side.

f.w: I will raise up thy lovers against thee

n: Babylon and its allies—Chaldeans, Pekod, Shoa, Koa, and Assyrians—will come, impressive horsemen all.

f.g: Peoples east of the Tigris within the Babylonian empire; Pekod is known from Babylonian records.

n: They will come with chariots, wagons, and shields. God will let them judge her by their own harsh standards.

f.g: A large shield.

f.w: they shall judge thee according to their judgments
f.g: By their own brutal customs.

n: God’s jealous love, betrayed, will allow them to treat her with fury. Mutilation was a known punishment in the ancient Near East; here it pictures the brutal treatment of captives.

f.w: they shall take away thy nose and thine ears
f.g: A punishment practiced in Assyria and Egypt.

n: They will strip her of her clothing and fine jewelry.
Thus God will end her unfaithfulness and her longing for Egypt.

f.g: She will finally stop looking to Egypt for help.

n: God will hand her to those she now hates.

f.g: The Babylonians.

n: They will treat her with hatred, take everything she worked for, and leave her bare and exposed.

f.g: Seize the fruit of her work.

n: This happens because she chased the nations and defiled herself with their idols.
She walked in her sister’s path, so she will drink her sister’s cup.

f.g: A cup of judgment.

n: The cup is deep and wide—full of mockery and scorn.

f.g: Ridiculed.

n: She will be filled with drunken misery: the cup of horror and ruin—Samaria’s cup.

f.w: the cup of astonishment and desolation

n: She will drain it, gnaw its broken pieces, and tear at herself in despair.

f.g: Broken pottery fragments.

n: The root sin: “Because you have forgotten me and thrown me behind your back.” God was treated as something to discard.
God asks Ezekiel to judge both sisters and declare their detestable acts.

f.w: wilt thou judge Aholah and Aholibah?

n: Their crimes: idolatry pictured as adultery, bloodshed, and sacrificing the children they bore to God.

f.w: to pass for them through the fire

n: On the very same day, they defiled God’s temple and profaned his Sabbaths.

f.g: Mixing pagan worship and temple worship without shame.

n: After killing their children for idols, they walked straight into God’s temple—worshipping him with blood on their hands.

f.w: then they came the same day into my sanctuary

n: They sent for foreign envoys and prepared for them like a woman beautifying herself—bathing, painting her eyes, and wearing jewelry.

f.g: Applied eye makeup, as Jezebel did.

n: She reclined on a fine couch at a banquet table and set out God’s own incense and oil for her guests.
A carefree crowd surrounded her, including drunkards brought from the desert, who adorned the sisters with bracelets and crowns.

f.g: Probably “drunkards” (a similar Hebrew word); either way, rough desert visitors.

n: God remarks: even this worn-out adulteress still goes on with her unfaithfulness.

f.w: her that was old in adulteries
f.g: One worn out by long unfaithfulness.

n: Yet they kept coming to both sisters.

f.g: The two unfaithful sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem.

n: Righteous judges will sentence them as adulteresses and murderers, because that is what they are.

f.w: the righteous men, they shall judge them
f.g: Even the nations used as God’s instruments act “righteously” in carrying out his sentence here.

n: God will bring an army against them to terrorize and plunder.

f.g: To be tossed about and looted.

n: The army will stone them, cut them down, kill their children, and burn their houses—the legal penalties for adultery and idolatry, carried out in war.
This will end such unfaithfulness in the land and serve as a warning to all.

f.w: that all women may be taught
f.g: That all may learn from their example.

n: They will bear the consequences of their idolatry—and in that they will come to know the Lord GOD.

f.w: ye shall bear the sins of your idols
